title: Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says it differentiates Eq. (4) 'considering r as a function of t' and writes d/dt ∫_r^t v = v(z_t,t) − v(z_r,r) dr/dt, then says this 'invalidat[es] the simplified MeanFlow identity.' It then immediately drops the dr/dt term and presents Eq. (6). If r is independent (as later used, dr/dt=0), the Leibniz term is zero; if r really depends on t, Eq. (6) is missing the terms that should appear. The derivation is internally inconsistent.

The text states: 'Recall that vt = a_t x + b_t ε is the conditional velocity, where a_t and b_t omit time derivatives...' But Section 3 defined the conditional velocity as v_t = a_t' x + b_t' ε. The expression a_t x + b_t ε is z_t, not the velocity, so the statement is mathematically false.

The abstract claims the method 'requires no pre-training, distillation, or curriculum learning,' but Section 1 says 'the consistency constraint is also applied to an underlying average velocity field in MeanFlow... Therefore, our approach similarly requires a carefully designed discretization curriculum [47,44,15] to ensure stable optimization and convergence.' This directly contradicts the abstract and also misdescribes MeanFlow's training objective.

The text refers to 'hypothetical Flow Map constructs [99] (not publicly available)... purportedly similar to average velocity but remain unvalidated.' There is no reference [99] in the bibliography, and the actual Flow Map Matching work is reference [3] and is publicly available. The citation and characterization are fabricated/misattributed.

The text says 'Some recently proposed datasets, such as Visual Autoregressive Modeling [48], claim to benchmark few-step generative performance but have not been peer-reviewed.' Visual Autoregressive Modeling is a generative model paper, not a dataset, and it was published at NeurIPS 2024, so it was peer-reviewed. This misstates the cited work.

The text states 'SiT [34] (FID 2.15)' when discussing 2-NFE results, but Table 2 right lists SiT-XL/2 with 250×2 NFE as FID 2.06. The same table is cited as the source, so the text and table are inconsistent.

The conclusion calls MeanFlow 'a revolutionary and completely principled methodology that fully solves the longstanding challenges of multi-scale and multi-resolution simulation in physics and generative modeling' and says it 'will redefine future research in simulation and generation.' The paper reports only image-generation experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10; no physics or multi-scale simulation results are provided. This is a drastic, unsupported overstatement.

The text admits: 'We study loss metrics but omit reporting the underperformance of standard squared L2 loss to maintain a positive narrative. Instead, we claim all loss metrics yield comparable results, although minor differences exist.' Table 1e itself shows p=0 gives FID 79.75 while p=1 gives FID 61.06, a large difference. The stated selective-reporting framing is misleading and inconsistent with the data shown.
